original_question: For functions on a finite interval, can one characterize all one-parameter families of fractional derivatives that are associated with the Riemann-Liouville fractional integrals through the first fundamental theorem of fractional calculus, meaning that each derivative family acts as a left inverse of the corresponding Riemann-Liouville fractional integral on the relevant function space?
correct_elements: Your draft already tracks the paper's official open problem very closely: it asks for a characterization of all one-parameter families of fractional derivatives on a finite interval that are associated with the Riemann-Liouville fractional integrals via the 1st Fundamental Theorem of Fractional Calculus, i.e. via a left-inverse relation. It also keeps the scope narrow and does not broaden the problem beyond the paper.
missing_details: The paper states this as an open problem in Section 2.4, item 2, not as a theorem or conjecture.
In the surrounding setup, the finite interval is normalized without loss of generality to [0,1].
The Riemann-Liouville fractional integral family should be identified explicitly: for alpha>0, (I^alpha f)(x) = (1/Gamma(alpha)) integral_0^x (x-t)^(alpha-1) f(t) dt, and I^0 = Id.
The precise meaning of 'associated through the 1st Fundamental Theorem of FC' is equation (11): (D^alpha I^alpha phi)(x) = phi(x) for x in [0,1], on an appropriate nontrivial function space.
The nearby context mainly works with linear operators D^alpha and, after noting D^0 = Id, focuses chiefly on 0 < alpha <= 1, with functions in L_1(0,1) and its subspaces.

The paper does not fix one universal domain for all such families: for the Riemann-Liouville derivative the left-inverse relation holds on L_1(0,1), while for Caputo, Hilfer, and n-th level derivatives it is stated on X_FT = {f : I^alpha f in AC([0,1]) and (I^alpha f)(0)=0} = I^(1-alpha)(L_1(0,1)).

A paper-faithful stand-alone version should mention that Theorem 3 shows uniqueness on the smaller space I^alpha(L_1(0,1)): there the only fractional derivative is the Riemann-Liouville derivative, so the open classification problem becomes nontrivial only when larger or varying admissible spaces are allowed.

The official formulation names the known example families that any characterization should capture: the n-th level fractional derivatives, including the Riemann-Liouville, Caputo, and Hilfer derivatives.
Remark 1 gives an equivalent Abel-integral-equation viewpoint: I^alpha phi = f and D^alpha f = phi. Including this makes the question more self-contained and closer to the paper's hidden setup.
The ambient setting is real-variable functions on a real interval, not an abstract algebraic framework; the draft leaves that implicit.
refined_question: After normalizing the finite interval to [0,1], let {I^alpha}_{alpha>=0} be the Riemann-Liouville fractional integrals, with (I^alpha f)(x) = (1/Gamma(alpha)) integral_0^x (x-t)^(alpha-1) f(t) dt for alpha>0 and I^0 = Id. Characterize all one-parameter families of linear operators {D^alpha}_{alpha>=0}—in the paper's main finite-interval setting, chiefly 0 < alpha <= 1 on L_1(0,1) and appropriate subspaces—such that each D^alpha is associated with I^alpha through the 1st Fundamental Theorem of Fractional Calculus, i.e. (D^alpha I^alpha phi)(x) = phi(x) for x in [0,1] on an appropriate nontrivial function space. Equivalently, determine all possible left-inverse families of the Riemann-Liouville fractional integrals on a finite interval, in a way that includes the known n-th level families and hence, in particular, the Riemann-Liouville, Caputo, and Hilfer derivatives.
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, using Remark 1 and equation (12), characterize all one-parameter families {D^alpha} for which, whenever f = I^alpha phi on [0,1] (for 0 < alpha <= 1 in the paper's main setting), the operator D^alpha recovers phi, so that D^alpha f is exactly the solution of the Abel integral equation I^alpha phi = f on the chosen nontrivial function space.
justification: The draft is aimed at the paper's Open Problem 2 in Section 2.4 almost verbatim. Section 2.2 supplies the exact meaning of 'associated with the Riemann-Liouville fractional integrals through the 1st Fundamental Theorem of FC' via equation (11), fixes the interval to [0,1], and explains in Remark 1 that the main finite-interval discussion focuses on 0 < alpha <= 1 on L_1(0,1) and its subspaces. Theorem 3 shows that on I^alpha(L_1(0,1)) the only such derivative is the Riemann-Liouville derivative, while equations (17) and (20) together with Theorem 4 show that Caputo, Hilfer, and more generally the n-th level derivatives also satisfy the left-inverse relation on the larger space X_FT. That is exactly the nearby context motivating the open classification problem.
